questions.prompt: Let f:{z:|z|<1}→{z:|z|≤1/2} be holomorphic with f(0)=0. Which statements are true?

questions.theory: Schwarz’s lemma applies to a holomorphic map of the unit disk into itself that fixes zero. It gives|h(z)|≤|z| and|h′(0)|≤1, with equality forcing a rotation. A map bounded by a smaller radius R is normalized by dividing by R, which yields|f(z)|≤R|z| when f(0)=0. A closed-disk range is harmless: a nonconstant holomorphic function cannot attain its maximum modulus inside the disk, and the constant case can be checked separately. The bound from the codomain is often weaker than the bound obtained by combining it with a fixed point. Evaluating the strongest inequality at the specified point can rule out a proposed value immediately. Multiple correct options may include both a sharp bound and a weaker consequence.

A universal claim must hold for all entire functions; the simplest nonconstant test f(z)=z often reveals the obstruction. questions.prompt: Which statements are correct?

options.A: Every group of order244 contains a unique subgroup of order27.
options.B: Every group of order1694 contains a unique subgroup of order121.
options.C: There exists a group of order154 containing a unique subgroup of order7.
options.D: There exists a group of order121 containing two subgroups of order11.

For existential claims, cyclic groups and a two-dimensional vector space over a prime field are useful examples.
questions.solution: A is false because27 does not divide244=4·61, so no subgroup of that order exists by Lagrange. For B,1694=2·7·11². The number n₁₁ of Sylow11-subgroups divides14 and is1 mod11. Among1,2,7,14 only1 qualifies; the order121 subgroup is unique. C is true: the cyclic group C₁₅₄ has exactly one subgroup of every divisor order, in particular7. D is true: C₁₁×C₁₁ has distinct subgroups generated by(1,0) and(0,1), both order11. In fact it has12 such subgroups; the printed statement says “contains two,” not “exactly two.” Hence B,C,D.
questions.theory: Lagrange’s theorem requires a subgroup’s order to divide the finite group’s order. Sylow’s theorems guarantee subgroups of maximal prime-power order and constrain their count n_p by n_p≡1 modulo p and n_p dividing the complementary factor. If only one divisor satisfies both conditions, the Sylow subgroup is unique and normal. A cyclic group has exactly one subgroup for each divisor of its order, providing convenient existence examples. The elementary abelian group C_p×C_p is a two-dimensional vector space overℤ/pℤ; its order-p subgroups are lines, numbering(p²−1)/(p−1)=p+1. Universal statements require every group, while existential statements need only one example. “Contains two” asserts at least two distinct subgroups unless exactness is explicitly stated; replacing it by “exactly two” changes the claim.

options.A: If G₁ is cyclic, G₂ is cyclic.
options.B: If G₁ is abelian, G₂ is abelian.

questions.solution: If G₁=⟨g⟩, surjectivity gives G₂=⟨φ(g)⟩, proving A. For target a=φ(x),b=φ(y), ab=φ(xy)=φ(yx)=ba when G₁ is abelian, proving B. φ(H) contains the identity and is closed under products and inverses, so C holds even without surjectivity. For D, choose a=φ(g)∈G₂; then aφ(N)a^{−1}=φ(gNg^{−1})=φ(N) by normality. Thus D holds. Surjectivity is essential to promote normality from the image φ(G₁) to all of G₂; it is also needed for cyclicity and commutativity of the whole target. All four assertions are true.
questions.theory: A group homomorphism preserves multiplication, identity, inverses and integer powers. Its image is a subgroup, and the image of any subgroup remains a subgroup by the same closure properties. When the homomorphism is onto, target elements can be lifted to source elements, allowing properties such as cyclicity and abelianness to pass to the whole target. Normality means invariance under every conjugation, and lifting a conjugating element proves a surjective image of a normal subgroup is normal. Without surjectivity, that image is guaranteed normal only inside the image group, not inside an arbitrary larger target. The first isomorphism theorem expresses this structure as G₁/kerφ≅G₂ for onto φ. Properties of quotients must not be reversed: an abelian target does not force an abelian source.

options.B: Δ is a subgroup of Sₙ×Sₙ.

The diagonal subgroup is normal precisely when the original group is abelian; conjugation by(a,e) exposes this condition. Likewise the multiplication map(a,b)↦ab is a homomorphism from G×G to G exactly for abelian G, because interchanging factors from the two components requires commutativity. Symmetric groups are abelian only for n≤2; primality of n does not provide commutativity, as S₃ demonstrates. Universal quantifiers include all positive n, so properties valid in small cases do not settle the question. A subgroup’s existence and its normality are separate statements, requiring closure and conjugation checks respectively.

questions.prompt: Which ideals are maximal inℤ[X]?
hints: Reduce the quotient modulo the given prime.
A quadratic over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root in that field.
questions.solution: ℤ[X]/(p,h)≅𝔽_p[X]/(h mod p), which is a field exactly when h mod p is irreducible. Over𝔽₂, X²+1=(X+1)², so A is not maximal. X²+X+1 has values1 at both0 and1, hence no root and is irreducible, proving B. Over𝔽₃, X²+1 takes values1,2,2 at0,1,2, so it is irreducible, proving C. But X²+X+1=(X−1)² over𝔽₃, so D is not maximal. The valid quotients are fields of4 and9 elements; the invalid ones contain a nonzero nilpotent residue from the repeated linear factor. Thus B,C.
questions.theory: An ideal M in a commutative unital ring is maximal exactly when the quotient ring R/M is a field. For an ideal(p,h(X)) inℤ[X] with prime p, first quotienting by p reduces coefficients to the finite field𝔽_p; the remaining quotient is by the polynomial h modulo p. In a polynomial ring over a field, a nonconstant polynomial generates a maximal ideal precisely when it is irreducible. For degrees two and three, irreducibility is equivalent to having no field root, making direct evaluation sufficient. This root test does not suffice for higher degrees, where factors can both have degree at least two. A repeated factor creates a nonzero nilpotent in the quotient and prevents it from being a field. Reduction can radically change factorization, so irreducibility overℚ is not the relevant criterion.

questions.prompt: Let E/F be a finite algebraic Galois extension with group G. Which statements are true?

options.A: There is an intermediate K≠F,E such that K/F is Galois.
options.B: If every proper intermediate K is Galois over F, then G is abelian.
options.C: If there are exactly three intermediate fields including F,E, then G is abelian.
options.D: If[E:F]=99, every intermediate field is Galois over F.

hints: Translate intermediate fields into subgroups, and Galois intermediate extensions into normal subgroups.
Not every group whose subgroups are all normal is abelian; also factor99.
questions.solution: A fails for E=ℚ(√2),F=ℚ, a degree2 Galois extension with no proper intermediate field. B fails for a Galois group Q₈: all its subgroups are normal, yet it is nonabelian. Such an extension exists explicitly by taking E=ℚ(t_g:g∈Q₈), letting Q₈ permute variables regularly, and F=E^{Q₈}; Artin’s fixed-field theorem gives[E:F]=8 and Galois group Q₈. For C, the correspondence gives exactly three subgroups:1,G and one proper nontrivial H. Any g outside H must generate G, because its subgroup cannot be1 orH. Hence G is cyclic, therefore abelian (indeed of order p²). For D,|G|=99=3²·11. Sylow11 and Sylow3 counts are both1: they divide9 and11 respectively and satisfy the relevant congruences. G is the product of abelian groups of orders11 and9, hence abelian. Every subgroup is normal, so every intermediate field is Galois. Thus C,D.
questions.theory: The fundamental theorem of finite Galois theory gives an inclusion-reversing bijection K↔Gal(E/K) between intermediate fields and subgroups of G. An intermediate extension K/F is Galois exactly when its corresponding subgroup is normal, with group the quotient. Consequently an abelian Galois group makes every intermediate extension Galois, but the converse need not hold: nonabelian Dedekind groups such as Q₈ have all subgroups normal. The number of fields equals the number of subgroups, including endpoints. A group with exactly one proper nontrivial subgroup is cyclic by choosing an element outside that subgroup, and then has prime-square order. Artin’s theorem constructs finite Galois extensions from faithful finite groups of field automorphisms, providing counterexamples without a memorized number-field polynomial. Sylow theory controls the degree99 case.

questions.prompt: Which statements are correct?

options.A: Open right half-planes form a basis for the Euclidean topology onℝ².
options.B: Lines parallel to the Y-axis form a basis for the dictionary order topology onℝ².
options.C: Open rectangles form a basis for the Euclidean topology onℝ².
options.D: Line segments without endpoints parallel to the Y-axis form a basis for the dictionary order topology onℝ².

hints: A basis must provide arbitrarily small neighborhoods inside every open set.
In lexicographic order, points with the same first coordinate have vertical intervals between them.
questions.solution: A is false: an open right half-plane containing a point cannot fit inside a bounded Euclidean ball around it. C is true: open rectangles are Euclidean-open, and a sufficiently small rectangle around any point fits inside any containing ball. In dictionary order,(x,y)<(x′,y′) iff x<x′ or x=x′ and y<y′. The interval between(x,a),(x,b) is exactly{x}×(a,b), so the vertical open segments are open and refine every order neighborhood, proving D. Entire vertical lines are open unions of segments but cannot refine a short vertical segment around a point; hence they are not a basis and B fails. Thus C,D.
questions.theory: A topological basis is a family of open sets such that every open neighborhood of every point contains a basis member containing that point. Covering the space alone is not enough; the local refinement condition distinguishes a genuine basis from a family of large open sets. Euclidean rectangles satisfy that condition because balls and rectangles can be fitted inside one another locally. In the dictionary, or lexicographic, order onℝ², the first coordinate is compared before the second. Since the second coordinate has no endpoints, each point has order intervals whose two endpoints share its first coordinate; these are vertical open segments. Thus each vertical line is an open component, but whole lines are too large to refine all neighborhoods. The order topology differs substantially from the Euclidean product topology.

similar_questions.prompt: Why do open disks form a basis for the usual topology onℝ²?
similar_questions.solution: The metric topology is defined by unions of open balls. Given a point in an open set, some disk about it lies inside that set, which is exactly the basis refinement property.

similar_questions.prompt: Is{x}×ℝ open in the lexicographic order topology onℝ²?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. It is the union over integers n≥1 of vertical intervals{x}×(−n,n), each an order interval. It is not Euclidean-open because it contains no Euclidean ball.

questions.prompt: Let X=∏ₙ₌₁∞[0,1], and define d(x,y)=supₙ≥1|xₙ−yₙ|/2ⁿ. Which statements are true?

options.A: The metric topology is finer than the product topology.
options.B: The metric topology is coarser than the product topology.
options.C: The metric topology equals the product topology.
options.D: The two topologies are not comparable.

hints: The exponentially small weights make all sufficiently late coordinates automatically negligible.
Show a finite-coordinate neighborhood fits inside each metric ball and a metric ball fits inside each product neighborhood.
questions.solution: Givenε>0 choose N with2^{−N−1}<ε. A product neighborhood imposing|xₙ−yₙ|<ε2ⁿ for n≤N lies in B_d(x,ε), since later weighted differences are at most2^{−N−1}. Conversely, for a basic product neighborhood constraining finitely many coordinates n∈F by|xₙ−yₙ|<δₙ, choose r<min_{n∈F}δₙ/2ⁿ. Then B_d(x,r) lies inside that neighborhood. Thus the topologies coincide, proving C and refuting D. Under the standard definitions, “finer” means containing the other topology and “coarser” means being contained in it, both allowing equality. Hence A and B also hold. If the words were intended to mean strictly finer or strictly coarser, only C would hold, but “strictly” is absent from the printed options. The graded set uses the standard non-strict definitions.
questions.theory: The product topology has basic neighborhoods restricting finitely many coordinates and leaving every other coordinate unrestricted. A metric constructed with weights tending to zero can reproduce this topology when each coordinate space has a uniformly bounded metric. Here|xₙ−yₙ|≤1, so an unrestrained tail contributes at most a small geometric weight; controlling finitely many initial coordinates controls the entire weighted supremum. Coordinate projections are continuous in the metric because|xₙ−yₙ|≤2ⁿd(x,y). These two observations prove both inclusions of topologies. By standard terminology, a topology is finer when it contains another and coarser when it is contained in another, with equality satisfying both relations. “Strictly finer” excludes equality and must be distinguished. The unweighted supremum metric would instead give a genuinely finer topology.

similar_questions.prompt: Do standard coordinate vectors e_k converge to0 in this weighted metric?
similar_questions.solution: d(e_k,0)=2^{−k}→0, so yes. They also converge coordinatewise to0, agreeing with the product topology.

similar_questions.prompt: Do e_k converge to0 under the unweighted supremum metric on[0,1]^ℕ?

questions.prompt: Let f∈C¹(ℝ) be bounded. For(P):x′(t)=f(x(t)), t>0, x(0)=0, which statements are true?

options.A: There are solutions defined for all t>0.

hints: C¹ regularity gives local Lipschitz continuity and uniqueness.
A global bound on f bounds both the displacement on finite time intervals and the solution’s slope.
questions.solution: Since f is C¹ it is locally Lipschitz, so local existence and uniqueness hold. Let|f|≤M. Then|x(t)−x(s)|≤M|t−s| wherever the solution exists, proving global Lipschitz regularity of the trajectory. On a finite maximal interval[0,T),|x(t)|≤Mt, so the trajectory stays bounded and is Cauchy as t↑T. Its finite limiting value permits local continuation past T, a contradiction. Therefore the unique solution exists for every t≥0, proving A,B,D. C contradicts uniqueness. Boundedness of f′ is not required: the trajectory’s Lipschitz constant comes from the bound on f itself, while f′ supplies only local uniqueness.
questions.theory: Picard–Lindelöf gives local existence and uniqueness for a continuous right-hand side locally Lipschitz in the state. A C¹ scalar function is locally Lipschitz by the mean value theorem on compact intervals. Extending local solutions yields a maximal interval, and finite-time failure on the full real state space can occur only if the trajectory becomes unbounded. A globally bounded velocity rules this out because|x(t)|≤|x(0)|+Mt on every finite time interval. The same integral identity gives|x(t)−x(s)|≤M|t−s|, making the solution globally Lipschitz as a function of time. This does not assert that f is globally Lipschitz in its argument; a bounded C¹ function may have an unbounded derivative. These are different uses of Lipschitz continuity and support different conclusions.

similar_questions.solution: x≡0 solves the equation. The function sin x is globally Lipschitz, so uniqueness forces this solution for all time.

similar_questions.solution: No. The right-hand side is C¹ but unbounded. Separation gives x=1/(1−t), which blows up at t=1. The missing bounded-velocity hypothesis is essential.

options.C: There is more than one solution.
options.D: g is Lipschitz in u in some neighborhood of0 and therefore the IVP has a unique solution.

questions.solution: For any fixed t≠0, |g(t,u)−g(t,0)|/|u|=t²|u|^{−4/5}→∞. Thus no neighborhood of the initial point has a uniform Lipschitz bound in u, proving A and refuting D. The zero solution proves B false. For any a≥0, define u_a(t)=0 for t≤a and u_a(t)=[(4/15)(t³−a³)]^{5/4} for t>a. Separating the nonzero branch gives(5/4)u^{4/5}=t³/3−a³/3. The branch derivative tends to0 at a, so the glued function is C¹ and satisfies the ODE there as well. questions.theory: Local Lipschitz continuity in the state is sufficient for uniqueness of an ODE solution, but failure of that condition does not by itself prove nonuniqueness; explicit distinct solutions do. Fractional powers u^α with0<α<1 have unbounded slope relative to u at zero and commonly permit waiting-time solutions. Separating variables on a nonzero branch must not discard the equilibrium branch that division removes. A branch can be glued to the zero solution at a time a when its derivative tends to zero, giving a classical solution. The factor t² vanishes at the single initial time, but a Lipschitz condition must hold on a time neighborhood, which includes nonzero times. The odd fifth root is real for negative u, allowing symmetric positive and negative departing branches. Peano’s continuity theorem still gives local existence.

Starting at y(0)=0 gives y(t)≤0, hence y≡0. It is the unique forward solution, proving B and refuting D. questions.theory: The standard local Lipschitz condition is sufficient for uniqueness, but its failure does not imply uniqueness must fail. The domain of a real square root imposes nonnegativity, which combines with the sign of the derivative to constrain trajectories. For x′=√x, a solution may remain at the equilibrium zero for an arbitrary time and then follow a separated positive branch. For y′=−√y starting at zero, forward motion cannot increase, while nonnegativity prevents a decrease, forcing the equilibrium. Time direction matters: reversing time interchanges these behaviors. Waiting-time formulas must be checked at the joining point, including differentiability there. Dividing by√x during separation would discard the equilibrium solution and conceal the family. A direct monotonicity argument can prove uniqueness without the usual theorem.

Since1/t has bounded second derivative on[1,2],Tₙ=log2+O(n^{−2}). Hence aₙ=log2−1/(4n)+O(n^{−2}), and|aₙ−log2|/bₙ→1/4. questions.theory: A convergence rate describes how the error relative to the limit decays, not the magnitude of the sequence itself. Two errors have the same asymptotic rate when their ratio tends to a finite positive constant, or more broadly when they have matching asymptotic order. Riemann sums for a smooth function usually have first-order endpoint error, while the composite trapezoidal rule has second-order error under a bounded second derivative. Adding half the difference of endpoint contributions converts a right-endpoint sum into a trapezoidal sum and isolates its leading error. Here the width is1/n and the endpoint values are1 and1/2, giving coefficient1/4. The exact harmonic-number expression H_{2n}−H_n gives the same expansion. Comparing aₙ itself with1/n would be wrong because aₙ converges to a nonzero constant.

Its solution with y(0)=1,y′(0)=1/2 is y=e^{x/2} on[0,1], which also makes the nonnegative integrand zero and is the global minimizer. It is strictly convex since y″=e^{x/2}/4>0; B is false. However the variational problem determines y only on[0,1], while C quantifies sums up to2. These values are undefined for a function on[0,1], or unrestricted for an arbitrary extension. A smooth extension agreeing with e^{x/2} through1 can violate C beyond1 without changing J. Endpoint conditions must then be imposed, and free endpoints may add natural boundary conditions. An ODE solution has a natural continuation, but that continuation is an extra assumption if extremality was imposed only on an interval. Restricting the identity to sums≤1 would make the intended statement well-defined and true.

questions.solution: Because the integrand does not depend on y,z themselves, Euler–Lagrange gives d(2y′+z′)/dx=0 and d(y′+2z′)/dx=0. Thus2y″+z″=0,y″+2z″=0, whose coefficient matrix has determinant3, so y″=z″=0. The endpoint values determine y=1−x and z=−1+3x. Then z+3y=2 and y+z=2x, proving A,C. The expression3z+y=−2+8x is not constantly2, refuting B; y+z differs from x for x≠0, refuting D. The positive-definite derivative quadratic also ensures this stationary pair is the unique minimizer.
questions.theory: For functionals involving several unknown functions, each component has its own Euler–Lagrange equation. If the integrand depends only on derivatives, these equations express conservation of the corresponding conjugate momenta. A positive-definite quadratic derivative form gives an invertible coefficient matrix, so constant momenta force constant derivatives and affine extremals. Endpoint data then determine these affine functions uniquely. Here the derivative form a²+b²+ab equals(a+b/2)²+3b²/4, strictly positive away from zero; this also provides strict convexity and uniqueness of the minimum with fixed endpoints. Linear combinations of the resulting functions should be checked as identities, not at just one point. A combination agreeing at one endpoint can still fail elsewhere. questions.theory: A finite-rank, or degenerate, integral kernel written asΣa_j(x)b_j(t) maps every function into the finite span of the a_j. questions.solution: Continuity and compactness give k=max_{[0,1]²}|K|<1. Let Tf(x)=∫K(x,y)f(y)dy. It maps C[0,1] to itself and satisfies‖Tf‖∞≤k‖f‖∞. Hence A,D are false, B is true because every continuous g works, and C is true as a special case of uniqueness for all continuous g. No differentiability of K or g is needed for existence or uniqueness in C[0,1].
questions.theory: The Banach fixed-point theorem gives a unique fixed point for a contraction on a complete metric space. C[0,1] with the supremum norm is complete, and a continuous integral kernel defines a bounded linear operator on it. On an interval of length one, a uniform kernel bound k gives operator norm at most k. A strict pointwise bound below one becomes a uniform strict bound only because the kernel is continuous on a compact set and attains its maximum. When‖T‖<1, the Neumann seriesΣ(−T)^j converges in operator norm and inverts I+T, yielding a solution for every right-hand side. Higher regularity is unrelated to uniqueness here. If the interval were longer, its length would multiply the crude bound and the contraction conclusion would require adjustment.

questions.theory: The momentum conjugate to a generalized coordinate q_j is p_j=∂L/∂q̇_j, taking other coordinates and velocities as independent variables. A point transformation x=x(q) changes the velocity by the chain rule and transforms momenta covariantly: p_j=Σp_xi∂x_i/∂q_j. Here p_x=ẏ and p_y=ẋ because the kinetic term is a cross product, so the radial momentum is p_xcosθ+p_ysinθ. questions.solution: For a standard normal,E[X⁴]=3 and E[X⁸]=105, so Var(X⁴)=105−9=96. The law of large numbers gives Yₙ/n→3 in probability. Thus A tends to0 and C tends to1. Let Zₙ=(Yₙ−3n)/√(96n); the CLT gives Zₙ⇒N(0,1). In B the standardized interval is[−2√(n/96),0], whose lower endpoint tends to−∞, so its probability tends toΦ(0)=1/2. In D it is[0,2√(n/96)], whose upper endpoint tends to∞, also giving1/2. The remote-tail probabilities vanish by Chebyshev or the law of large numbers. Therefore B,D.

Normal even moments satisfy E[X^{2k}]=(2k−1)!!, giving the required fourth and eighth moments. An interval entirely a fixed fraction below the mean has limiting probability zero; one containing a fixed-fraction neighborhood around the mean has probability one. If one boundary is exactly the mean and the other is macroscopically far away, asymptotic normal symmetry gives one half. questions.prompt: Let A,B be events in a discrete probability space with P(A)>0,P(B)>0. Which statements are necessarily true?

For B,D, use a finite four-point space with masses0.2,0.6,0.1,0.1, let B be the first point and A the first two. Then a=0.8,b=c=0.2. We have P(A|B)=1, but P(B|A)=0.25≠1, refuting B. Also1>P(B)=0.2 while0.25 is not greater than P(A)=0.8, refuting D. Thus A,C.
questions.theory: Conditional probability is P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) when the conditioning event has positive probability. Both directions share the same intersection numerator but generally have different denominators. A zero conditional probability is symmetric because it means the intersection is null. Conditional probability one means B is contained in A up to a null set, not that A is contained in B. Positive association P(A|B)>P(A) is symmetric after cross-multiplication, equivalent to P(A∩B)>P(A)P(B), or positive covariance of the two event indicators. Comparing P(A|B) with P(B) instead of P(A) yields a different inequality with no such symmetry. questions.prompt: For n≥2, let P be a transition matrix of a Markov chain on{1,…,n}, and Iₙ the identity. Which statements are necessarily true?

questions.solution: A finite chain has at least one closed communicating class, and every state in a finite closed irreducible class is positive recurrent, proving A. B is false: for P=I every state is absorbing and recurrent, with no transient state. C is false: take n=2,P=[[0,1],[1,0]]. The proposed matrix has diagonal entries−1/3, so it is not a transition matrix despite row sums1. For D, let1 be the all-ones column vector. Since P1=1 and P²1=1,(I+3P+P²)1=5·1. Thus5 is an eigenvalue, proving D. Hence A,D.
questions.theory: A transition matrix has nonnegative entries and each row sums to one. The all-ones vector is therefore a right eigenvector with eigenvalue one, and applying a polynomial in the matrix sends it to the polynomial evaluated at one times that vector. A finite Markov chain decomposes into communicating classes; at least one class is closed because the finite directed graph of classes has a sink. Finite closed irreducible classes are recurrent, while transient states may or may not exist outside them. Absorbing states are simple recurrent examples. A linear combination of stochastic matrices with nonnegative coefficients summing to one is stochastic, but a negative coefficient can destroy entrywise nonnegativity. Checking just row sums is insufficient. Recurrence is about eventual return probability, not merely a positive self-transition.

similar_questions.prompt: For P=[[1,0],[1/2,1/2]], classify the states.

similar_questions.prompt: Show7 is an eigenvalue of2I+P+4P² for a stochastic P.
similar_questions.solution: Apply the matrix to the all-ones vector:2·1+1+4·1=7·1. Thus it has eigenvalue7 regardless of the other eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,X₂ₙ, n≥1, be independent N(0,1) variables. Which statements are correct?

questions.solution: The numerator in A is normal with variance2n; dividing by2n gives variance1/(2n), not2, so A fails. The n disjoint differences are independent N(0,2). Dividing each by√2 gives independent standard normals, so the sum of their squares is2χₙ², proving B. For independent standard normals X,Y, both X+Y and X−Y have law N(0,2), whose absolute mean is√2·√(2/π)=2/√π. The pointwise identity max(|X|,|Y|)=(|X+Y|+|X−Y|)/2 therefore gives expectation2/√π, proving C and refuting D. No independence between the two sums is needed for this expectation identity, though they are independent in the normal case.
questions.theory: Independent centered normal variables remain normal under linear combinations, with variance equal to the sum of coefficient squares times component variances. A chi-square variable with n degrees of freedom is the sum of squares of n independent standard normals, so scaled normal differences must first be normalized. Disjoint pairs are independent because they use disjoint independent observations. For a centered normal of standard deviationσ, the absolute mean isσ√(2/π), obtained by integrating its symmetric density. The algebraic identity for the maximum of two absolute values converts an order-statistic expectation into two simple normal absolute moments. Linearity of expectation does not require the terms be independent. Index n+1 guarantees the two variables in the maximum are distinct even when n=1.

similar_questions.prompt: For independent N(0,1) variables X,Y, find the law of(X−Y)².

similar_questions.prompt: For independent N(0,σ²) variables X,Y, find E max(|X|,|Y|).

questions.prompt: Let X∼Uniform(−1,1) and Y=X². Which statements are NOT true?

options.D: X,Y are neither independent nor correlated.

questions.solution: EX=0,EY=EX²=1/3 and E[XY]=EX³=0, so Cov(X,Y)=0. Both variances are positive, hence their correlation is zero. They are nevertheless dependent: the event B={Y≤1/4} equals{|X|≤1/2} and has probability1/2. If X,Y were independent, this event belonging to both generated sigma-algebras would satisfy P(B)=P(B)², impossible for1/2. Thus the actual relationship is dependent and uncorrelated, making D true. The question asks for statements NOT true: A wrongly claims independence, B wrongly claims both independence and nonzero correlation, and C wrongly claims nonzero correlation. Select A,B,C.
questions.theory: Independence means probabilities factor for every pair of events determined by the two random variables. Uncorrelatedness means zero covariance when second moments exist and is substantially weaker outside the jointly normal family. For a symmetric distribution, expectations of integrable odd functions vanish, so X can be uncorrelated with an even nonlinear function such as X². Yet a nondegenerate deterministic function Y=h(X) cannot be independent of X: any event determined by Y is also determined by X, and independence would force its probability to be zero or one. Variance positivity ensures correlation is well-defined. The problem’s negative wording changes the requested answer set: select the three incorrect descriptions rather than the one correct description. A deterministic nonlinear relationship can therefore be completely invisible to Pearson correlation.

similar_questions.prompt: For X∼Uniform(0,1), compute Cov(X,X²).

questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,X₂ₙ be iid N(μ,1), independent of a standard Cauchy W. Which statistics are consistent for μ?

questions.solution: A has meanμ and variance1/n, so Chebyshev gives consistency. C is an average of n independent odd-indexed observations with the same moments and is also consistent. B has mean2μ and variance2/n, hence converges in probability to2μ; it is not an estimator consistent for μ throughout the parameter space, though it works accidentally atμ=0. For D, the sample-mean term tends toμ, and for everyε>0,P(|W|/n>ε)=P(|W|>nε)→0. Slutsky’s theorem gives consistency even though W has no mean or variance. With a single fixed W, W/n even tends to zero almost surely. Thus A,C,D.
questions.theory: Consistency means convergence in probability to the parameter for every parameter value in the model. An unbiased estimator with variance tending to zero is consistent by Chebyshev, but unbiasedness and finite variance are not necessary. A wrongly normalized sum may have vanishing variance around the wrong target, as the2n observations divided by n illustrate. Selecting a fixed fraction of an iid sample still gives a consistent average if the selected sample size tends to infinity. A perturbation converging to zero in probability preserves consistency by Slutsky. For any real-valued random variable W finite almost surely, W/n→0 in probability because its tail probabilities vanish; this needs no moments. One Cauchy contaminant divided by n differs fundamentally from averaging n independent Cauchy variables, whose distribution does not concentrate.

similar_questions.prompt: Is X̄ₙ+Z/n consistent for μ when Xᵢ have finite meanμ and Z is any finite real random variable?
similar_questions.solution: The law of large numbers gives X̄ₙ→μ in probability, and P(|Z|>nε)→0. Their sum therefore converges toμ in probability.

similar_questions.prompt: Is the average of n iid standard Cauchy variables consistent for0?
similar_questions.solution: No. Cauchy stability gives the same standard Cauchy distribution for every average. For fixedε>0 its probability of exceedingε in magnitude stays positive rather than tending to0.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true?

options.A: A maximum likelihood estimator may not be unique.
options.B: A complete statistic is always sufficient.
options.C: A sufficient statistic may not be complete.
options.D: Every function of a sufficient statistic is sufficient.

hints: Completeness concerns zero expectations, while sufficiency concerns retention of parameter information.
For a counterexample to arbitrary functions preserving sufficiency, take a constant function.
questions.solution: A is true: for one Uniform(θ,θ+1) observation x, every θ∈[x−1,x] maximizes the indicator likelihood, so the MLE is not unique. B is false: a constant statistic T=0 is complete because Eθh(T)=h(0)=0 forces h(T)=0, but it is not sufficient in a nontrivial normal-location model. C is true: with two iid N(μ,1) observations, the full sample T=(X₁,X₂) is sufficient, yet h(T)=X₁−X₂ has expectation0 for everyμ and is nonzero almost surely, so T is not complete. D is false: the constant function of the sufficient normal sample mean loses the information aboutμ and is not sufficient. One-to-one functions preserve sufficiency; arbitrary functions need not. Thus A,C.
questions.theory: A statistic is sufficient when the conditional distribution of the sample given it does not depend on the parameter; in dominated models the factorization theorem offers an equivalent criterion. It is complete when every integrable function of it with zero expectation for all parameter values is almost surely zero. These definitions address different properties, so neither automatically implies the other. A complete sufficient statistic is a stronger combination used in the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem for unique minimum-variance unbiased estimators. A one-to-one measurable transformation retains a statistic’s information and preserves sufficiency, but a many-to-one transformation may discard information. Likelihood maximizers can form a set rather than a single point, especially with flat likelihood regions. A complete constant statistic gives a simple counterexample to conflating completeness with informativeness.

similar_questions.prompt: For iid Bernoulli(p) observations, is the sum sufficient?
similar_questions.solution: The joint mass is p^{Σxᵢ}(1−p)^{n−Σxᵢ}. It factors through the sum, so the sum is sufficient by the factorization theorem.

similar_questions.prompt: For X∼N(μ,1), is the statistic X² sufficient forμ?
similar_questions.solution: No. Given X²=t>0, the relative probabilities of signs are proportional to exp(−(√t−μ)²/2) and exp(−(−√t−μ)²/2), whose ratio is exp(2μ√t). It depends onμ, so squaring the sufficient full observation loses information.

Its second moment is0.4(10+10²)+0.6(4+3²)=51.8, so VarY=51.8−5.8²=18.16, refuting C. Equivalently total variance is0.4·10+0.6·4+0.4·0.6(10−3)²=18.16. The independent weighted sum0.4X₁+0.6X₂ instead has variance0.4²·10+0.6²·4=3.04, different from the mixture variance, refuting D even as an equality in distribution. Thus A,B.
questions.theory: A mixture distribution has densityΣw_jf_j with nonnegative weights summing to one. It can be constructed by drawing a component label first and then drawing from that component, so its mean is the weighted average of component means. The law of total variance separates its variance into the average component variance plus the variance of component means. The second term is essential when the components have different centers. An arithmetic weighted sum of independent random variables is a different operation: its distribution is a convolution after scaling, and its variance uses squared weights. Equality of the means does not imply equality of the distributions. Component independence is not needed to specify the mixture density, but it determines the variance of the proposed weighted sum and makes the comparison decisive.

questions.prompt: Under null H, P(X=x)=1/20 for x=1,…,20; under alternative K, P(X=x)=x/210. Define φ(x)=1 if x≤2 and0 otherwise, and ψ(x)=1 if x≥19 and0 otherwise. Which statements are true?

options.D: The power of ψ exceeds the power of φ.

hints: A test function equal to1 indicates rejection. Compute its expectation under the null for size and under the alternative for power.
Both rejection regions contain two points, but their alternative masses differ greatly.
questions.solution: Under H each point has mass1/20, so sizeφ=2/20=0.1 and sizeψ=2/20=0.1. Thus A holds and B fails. Under K, powerφ=(1+2)/210=1/70, while powerψ=(19+20)/210=13/70≈0.1857. This is greater than0.05 and greater than1/70, proving C,D. The normalizationΣ₁²⁰x=210 ensures K is a probability law. The likelihood ratio q(x)/p(x)=2x/21 increases with x, explaining why the upper-tail test has greater power at the same size. Hence A,C,D.
questions.theory: A test function maps each possible observation to a rejection probability, with values zero or one for nonrandomized tests. Its size is the supremum of rejection probabilities over the null parameter set; for a simple null this is just its expectation under that one distribution. Power is rejection probability under an alternative distribution. Discrete spaces make these probabilities finite sums over the rejection region. Equal numbers of support points yield equal sizes under a uniform null, but need not yield equal powers under a nonuniform alternative. The Neyman–Pearson lemma says a most powerful test of a simple null against a simple alternative rejects for large likelihood ratio. Here the increasing ratio favors large observations, matching the explicit comparison. Size and power must not be interchanged, and endpoints included by≤ or≥ count.

similar_questions.prompt: On{1,…,10} with a uniform null, what is the size of rejecting when X≥9?

similar_questions.prompt: If the alternative mass is x/55 on that same support, find this test’s power.
similar_questions.solution: Power is(9+10)/55=19/55. It exceeds the power of rejecting at{1,2}, which is3/55, although both tests have size1/5.

questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid N(0,τ^{−2}), with τ^{−2}>0. Put a prior density on τ² proportional to(1/τ²)^α for α>0. Which statements are true?

options.A: The prior is improper for every α>0.
options.B: The posterior is proper for every α>0.
options.C: Under squared-error loss, the generalized Bayes estimator of τ² is(n/2−α)/(ΣᵢXᵢ²/2).
options.D: The posterior is proper for α=1.

hints: Use t=τ² as the positive precision parameter; the prior is t^{−α} with respect to dt.
The likelihood contributes t^{n/2}exp[−tΣXᵢ²/2], giving a gamma posterior when its shape is positive.
questions.solution: Write t=τ² and S=Σxᵢ². The prior integral∫₀∞t^{−α}dt diverges at0 ifα≥1 and at∞ ifα≤1; A holds. For S>0, the posterior kernel is t^{n/2−α}e^{−St/2}, a Gamma(shape a=n/2−α+1,rate S/2) density precisely when a>0. Thus B is false for sufficiently largeα. Under squared-error loss, when proper the posterior mean is a/(S/2)=(n/2−α+1)/(S/2), not C’s expression; the latter is the interior gamma mode when a>1. Forα=1, a=n/2>0 and the posterior is proper for every positive sample size almost surely, proving D. S=0 is a null-probability sample under the continuous model and would not normalize. Thus A,D.
questions.theory: An improper prior is a nonnegative prior kernel with infinite total mass; it may still yield a proper posterior after multiplication by the likelihood. Prior densities depend on the specified parameterization and reference measure, so a power prior on precision t must not be treated as the same power prior on variance1/t. For a known-zero-mean normal sample, the precision likelihood is t^{n/2}exp(−St/2). The gamma integral∫₀∞t^{a−1}e^{−bt}dt is finite exactly when a,b>0, determining posterior propriety. Under squared-error loss the Bayes action is the posterior mean, while a gamma mode uses shape minus one and exists in the interior only for shape>1. Improper prior calculations are called generalized Bayes procedures and require checking posterior normalization before reporting an estimator.

similar_questions.prompt: For n=4,S=8,α=1, find the posterior and Bayes estimate of precision.
similar_questions.solution: The shape is4/2−1+1=2 and rate4. The posterior is Gamma(2,4), whose mean is2/4=1/2 and mode(2−1)/4=1/4.

similar_questions.prompt: For n=2,α=3,S>0, is the posterior proper?
similar_questions.solution: Its shape would be1−3+1=−1. The kernel behaves like t^{−2} near0, whose integral diverges. Hence the posterior is improper despite exponential decay at∞.

questions.prompt: Let(X₁,Y₁),…,(X₄,Y₄) be a sample from a continuous bivariate law with no ties. To test independence against positive association, let K=Σ_{i<j}ψ((Xᵢ,Yᵢ),(Xⱼ,Yⱼ)), where ψ=1 for concordant pairs and−1 for discordant pairs. Which statements are true?
hints: Sort by X; under independence the Y ranks form a uniform permutation of four symbols.
There are six pairs. If D is the inversion count, K=6−2D.
questions.solution: After sorting X, the24 permutations of Y ranks are equally likely under H₀. Concordant pairs are noninversions and discordant pairs are inversions, so K=6−2D. K=6 corresponds to D=0, only the increasing permutation, giving P(K=6)=1/24, not1/12; D fails. K=4 corresponds to D=1. A single inversion is produced by swapping one adjacent pair in the increasing order:2134,1324,1243, so the probability is3/24, proving C. The event K≥4 consists of D≤1, with total probability(1+3)/24=1/6, proving B and refuting A. Thus B,C.
questions.theory: Kendall’s rank statistic compares every pair of observations by whether their coordinate orders agree or disagree. With no ties, each pair contributes±1, and for a sample of size m there are m(m−1)/2 pairs. Sorting one coordinate turns discordant pairs into inversions of the other coordinate’s rank permutation. Under continuous independent marginals, that permutation is uniform over m! possibilities, giving a distribution-free null law. Exact small-sample tail probabilities can therefore be counted combinatorially rather than approximated by a normal distribution. The unnormalized statistic here ranges from−6 to6 in steps of two; a normalized Kendall tau would divide by six. Perfect agreement has one permutation, while exactly one inversion has m−1 permutations. Distinguish a one-sided upper-tail probability from a two-sided probability, which can introduce a factor of two.

similar_questions.prompt: For three observations under independence, find P(K=3).
similar_questions.solution: There are3!=6 rank permutations and three pairs. K=3 requires no inversions, only the increasing permutation, so probability1/6.

similar_questions.prompt: For four observations, find P(|K|=6) under independence.
similar_questions.solution: K=6 is perfect agreement and K=−6 perfect reversal, each one of24 permutations. Thus the two-sided probability is2/24=1/12.

Find the nullspace of that matrix; estimable coefficient vectors must annihilate it.
questions.solution: The design rows are(2,−1,−1,0),(0,1,0,−1),(0,1,1,−2). Solving Xh=0 gives h₂=h₄,h₃=h₄,h₁=h₄, so kerX=span{(1,1,1,1)}. The row space is its orthogonal complement; hence a coefficient vector l is estimable iffΣlᵢ=0. The sums for A,B,C are0,0,0, whereas D’s sum is8, so A,B,C are estimable and D is not. Explicit unbiased linear estimators are8Y₁−2Y₂+Y₃ for A,−Y₂+Y₃ for B, and(57/2)Y₁−5Y₂+(31/2)Y₃ for C. Moving every βᵢ by the same amount leaves all observation means unchanged but changes D by eight times that amount, proving nonidentifiability directly.
questions.theory: In a linear model E(Y)=Xβ, a linear parametric function lᵀβ is estimable when there is a linear unbiased estimator aᵀY, requiring Xᵀa=l. This is equivalent to l belonging to the row space of X, or to l being orthogonal to every vector in kerX. The nullspace records parameter changes invisible in the observation means, so an estimable target must remain invariant under all such changes. Error variances affect the best estimator’s variance but not this basic estimability criterion. A deficient-rank design can still estimate many contrasts even when individual coefficients are unidentifiable. Checking the nullspace often simplifies several candidate functions at once. Constructing a vector a gives an explicit estimator and verifies the positive cases, while a null direction supplies a concrete proof of the negative case.

similar_questions.prompt: If E(Y)=β₁+β₂, are β₁ and β₁+β₂ estimable?
similar_questions.solution: The design row is(1,1) and kernel isspan{(1,−1)}. β₁ is not invariant along that kernel, hence not estimable. β₁+β₂ is estimated unbiasedly by Y.

similar_questions.prompt: If E(Y₁)=β₁−β₂ and E(Y₂)=β₂−β₃, estimate β₁−β₃.
similar_questions.solution: Adding the means gives β₁−β₃, so Y₁+Y₂ is unbiased. The target is a row-space contrast even though a common shift of all three coefficients is unidentifiable.

questions.prompt: Let Y=Xβ+ε, with n>5, rankX=5, β=(β₀,…,β₄)ᵀ, and independent N(0,1) errors. Test H₀:β₁=β₂=β₃=β₄=c, a known constant, against its negation. Which statements are true?

options.A: The sum of squared residuals under H₀ has a central χ² distribution with n−5 degrees of freedom.
options.B: The sum of squared residuals under H₀ has a central χ² distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom.
options.C: The test statistic has a central F distribution with(5,n−1) degrees of freedom.
options.D: The test statistic has a central F distribution with(4,n−5) degrees of freedom.

hints: Under the constrained null model only β₀ is free after subtracting the four known contributions.
The difference between restricted and unrestricted residual sums of squares has four degrees of freedom.
questions.solution: Let RSS₀ denote the residual sum of squares fitting the constrained null model, and RSS₁ that from the unrestricted five-parameter fit. Under H₀ subtract c times the sum of columns1–4 from Y; the remaining mean lies in the one-dimensional span of column0. Therefore RSS₀∼χ²_{n−1}, proving B and refuting A for the null-model residuals named in the option. The unrestricted RSS₁ instead has χ²_{n−5}, a different quantity. Orthogonal normal projections give RSS₀−RSS₁∼χ²₄ independent of RSS₁. Thus F=[(RSS₀−RSS₁)/4]/[RSS₁/(n−5)]∼F_{4,n−5}, proving D and refuting C. The two degrees of freedom correspond to four independent restrictions and five fitted full-model coefficients. Hence B,D.
questions.theory: For a Gaussian linear model with unit error variance, residual sum of squares from an r-dimensional fitted affine mean space has a central chi-square law with n−r degrees of freedom when the true mean belongs to that space. In nested models, the difference of residual sums of squares corresponds to an orthogonal projection onto the added directions, so it is independent of the full-model residual sum by normality. Testing q independent linear restrictions uses q numerator degrees of freedom and n−p denominator degrees of freedom for p full-model coefficients. Known nonzero restrictions are handled by subtracting a fixed mean offset; they do not consume fitted degrees of freedom. The phrase null-model residual sum must be distinguished from full-model residual sum evaluated under the null hypothesis. Here those laws have n−1 and n−5 degrees of freedom respectively.

similar_questions.prompt: In a full-rank model with p=3 coefficients and n observations, test two coefficients fixed at known values. Give the F law.
similar_questions.solution: There are q=2 independent restrictions. Under the null, the usual extra-sum-of-squares statistic has F_{2,n−3}; the restricted model has one free coefficient and RSS₀ has χ²_{n−1} for unit variance.

questions.prompt: Let X₁,…,Xₙ₊₁ be a sample from N_p(μ,Σ), with p>2,n>p+3 andΣ positive definite. Define X̄ₙ=(1/n)Σᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ and(n−1)S=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ(Xᵢ−X̄ₙ)(Xᵢ−X̄ₙ)ᵀ. Which statements are correct?
hints: For a normal sample the sample mean and sample covariance are independent; the extra observation is also independent of both.
The mean-minus-new-observation vector has covariance(1+1/n)Σ. Apply Wishart inverse and Hotelling quadratic-form identities.
questions.solution: Let D=X̄ₙ−Xₙ₊₁. Then D∼N_p(0,cΣ),c=(n+1)/n, independent of W=(n−1)S∼W_p(n−1,Σ). Thus DᵀΣ^{−1}D∼cχ_p², proving D. Whiten and divide D by√c to obtain Z∼N_p(0,I), independent of A=Σ^{−1/2}WΣ^{−1/2}∼W_p(n−1,I). The identity ZᵀA^{−1}Z∼[p/(n−p)]F_{p,n−p} gives DᵀS^{−1}D=c(n−1)[p/(n−p)]F, exactly A’s scale. Independence and ES=Σ give E[X̄ᵀSX̄]=E[X̄ᵀΣX̄]=tr(Σ·Σ/n)+μᵀΣμ, proving B. Finally E[W^{−1}]=Σ^{−1}/(n−p−2), so E[S^{−1}]=(n−1)Σ^{−1}/(n−p−2), proving C. The assumed n ensures the inverse and its expectation exist. All four hold.
questions.theory: For a multivariate normal sample of size n, the sample mean has law N_p(μ,Σ/n) and is independent of the unbiased sample covariance S, with(n−1)S Wishart of n−1 degrees of freedom. If W∼W_p(ν,Σ), its inverse mean exists forν>p+1 and equalsΣ^{−1}/(ν−p−1). For independent Z∼N_p(0,I) and A∼W_p(ν,I), the scaled quadratic form[(ν−p+1)/p]ZᵀA^{−1}Z has F_{p,ν−p+1} distribution. Whitening and variance normalization are essential before applying this identity. For a deterministic symmetric matrix M and vector Y with finite covariance V, E[YᵀMY]=tr(MV)+(EY)ᵀM(EY). Independence permits replacing a random S by its expectation in the displayed mixed quadratic form; without normal-sample independence that step would need justification.

similar_questions.prompt: For p=3,n=8,Σ=I, compute E[S^{−1}].
For independent X̄∼N_p(μ,Σ/n) and X_new∼N_p(μ,Σ), find the law of their known-covariance squared distance.
similar_questions.solution: Their difference is centered normal with covariance(1+1/n)Σ. Whitening gives p independent normals of variance(1+1/n), so the squared distance is((n+1)/n)χ_p².

questions.prompt: Let Yᵢ=α+βxᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,2,3, with fixed xᵢ and iid N(0,σ²) errors,σ²>0. Observations are(xᵢ,yᵢ)=(1,2.1),(2,3.9),(3,6). Which statements are true?

options.A: The maximum likelihood estimate of α is0.1.
options.B: The least-squares estimate of α is0.1.
options.C: The best linear unbiased estimate of α is0.1.
options.D: The maximum likelihood estimate of β/α is19.5.

hints: Compute the ordinary least-squares slope and intercept from centered sums.
Under normal homoscedastic errors, least squares, coefficient MLE and BLUE coincide; use MLE invariance for the ratio.
questions.solution: Here x̄=2,ȳ=4,S_xx=(−1)²+0²+1²=2, and S_xy=(−1)(2.1−4)+0+(1)(6−4)=3.9. Thus β̂=3.9/2=1.95 and α̂=4−1.95·2=0.1, proving B. Gaussian likelihood maximization in the coefficients minimizes the same residual sum of squares, proving A; Gauss–Markov makes that least-squares intercept BLUE, proving C. MLE invariance gives the ratio estimate β̂/α̂=1.95/0.1=19.5, proving D. Residuals are0.05,−0.1,0.05, with RSS=0.015>0, so the unknown-variance MLE also exists, atσ̂²=0.015/3=0.005. All options hold.
questions.theory: In a full-rank simple linear regression with intercept, ordinary least squares has slope S_xy/S_xx and intercept ȳ−β̂x̄. Independent equal-variance errors satisfy the Gauss–Markov assumptions, so these coefficient estimators are best linear unbiased estimators. Normal errors additionally make least squares the maximum likelihood estimator of the coefficients, even when the common variance is unknown, provided the residual sum is positive. The MLE of variance divides RSS by n, while an unbiased variance estimator divides by n−2. MLE invariance allows estimating a function of parameters by that function evaluated at the MLE; it does not confer unbiasedness or the BLUE property on nonlinear ratios. A ratio requires a nonzero estimated denominator, and the parameter function itself is meaningful only where the true denominator is nonzero. These data satisfy the relevant computational condition.

questions.prompt: For a nonnegative continuous random variable, which conditions hold for its cumulative hazard H(t)?
hints: Write H(t)=−logS(t), where S(t)=P(X>t) is the survival function.
A proper continuous nonnegative law has S(0)=1 and S(t)→0.
questions.solution: For a continuous nonnegative X, P(X=0)=0 and S(0)=P(X>0)=1, so H(0)=−log1=0, proving B. Since X is a proper finite real random variable, S(t)→0 as t→∞ and H(t)→∞, proving A, with H=∞ beyond any finite support endpoint if necessary. Survival is nonincreasing, so−logS is nondecreasing, proving D. C is not universal: an exponential law of rate2 has S(t)=e^{−2t},H(t)=2t, hence H(1)=2 rather than1. Cumulative hazard is not a CDF and is not normalized to equal one at any fixed time. Thus A,B,D.
questions.theory: The survival function of a nonnegative lifetime is S(t)=1−F(t), and its cumulative hazard is H(t)=−logS(t) wherever survival is positive. For an absolutely continuous law, the instantaneous hazard h=f/S integrates to H from zero. Continuity removes an atom at zero, giving the initial value H(0)=0. A proper lifetime distribution has survival tending to zero, so cumulative hazard diverges even when the instantaneous hazard is not monotone. Bounded-support distributions can have infinite cumulative hazard at a finite endpoint; the extended-real convention handles them. H is nondecreasing because survival decreases, but it is unbounded and is not a probability distribution function. A defective distribution with positive probability of infinite lifetime would have a finite limiting hazard and would fall outside the stated proper real-valued setting.

similar_questions.prompt: Find H for an exponential lifetime of rateλ>0.
similar_questions.solution: S(t)=e^{−λt} for t≥0, so H(t)=λt. It begins at0, increases, and diverges; H(1)=λ depends on the rate.

similar_questions.prompt: Find H for X∼Uniform(0,2).
similar_questions.solution: For0≤t<2,S(t)=1−t/2, so H(t)=−log(1−t/2). It tends to∞ as t↑2 and is taken as∞ for t≥2.

questions.prompt: Cars arrive at a petrol pump at rate10 per hour according to a Poisson process. A single staff member refills cars with independent exponential service times averaging4 minutes, and cars leave immediately after service. Let α be the probability of finding3 or more cars waiting to refill and β the mean number of cars in the queue. Which statements are correct?
hints: Convert the mean service time into an hourly service rate and compute utilization.
Distinguish the number in the entire system from the number waiting while a car is being served.
questions.solution: This is a stable M/M/1 model with λ=10/hour,μ=60/4=15/hour andρ=λ/μ=2/3. In equilibrium the system count N has P(N=k)=(1−ρ)ρ^k. If “queue” includes the car in service, α=P(N≥3)=ρ³=8/27 and β=EN=ρ/(1−ρ)=2. Then A,C are true because β−α=46/27, while B,D are false (αβ=16/27). If “waiting” excludes the car being refilled, the queue count Q=(N−1)^+ instead gives α=P(Q≥3)=P(N≥4)=ρ⁴=16/81 and β=EQ=ρ²/(1−ρ)=4/3. Then β−α=92/81 and αβ=64/243, so none of the printed options is true. The source uses waiting/queue without specifying whether service is included; the two customary counts change the answer set. No unconditional graded answer is assigned. The intended system-count answer is A,C.
questions.theory: An M/M/1 queue has Poisson arrivals, independent exponential service times and one server. In equilibrium it is stable whenρ=λ/μ<1, and detailed balance gives the geometric system-count distribution P(N=k)=(1−ρ)ρ^k. Its tail is P(N≥m)=ρ^m and its mean L=ρ/(1−ρ). The number waiting excludes a customer currently in service: Q=(N−1)^+, with mean L_q=ρ²/(1−ρ) and tail P(Q≥m)=ρ^{m+1} for m≥1. These quantities differ by server occupancy, whose mean isρ. Time units must match before computing utilization. Little’s law also distinguishes waiting time from total system time. The phrase queue can sometimes include service, while “waiting” usually excludes it; an exam item should define its count explicitly when the options depend on that distinction.

similar_questions.prompt: For an M/M/1 system withλ=3,μ=5 per hour, find mean system and waiting counts.
similar_questions.solution: ρ=3/5. L=ρ/(1−ρ)=3/2. L_q=ρ²/(1−ρ)=9/10. Their difference isρ=3/5, the mean indicator of a busy server.

similar_questions.prompt: For the same system, compare probabilities of at least two in the system and at least two waiting.
similar_questions.solution: P(N≥2)=ρ²=9/25. At least two waiting means N≥3, so P(Q≥2)=ρ³=27/125. Excluding service shifts the geometric-tail exponent by one.
